lesson.title: konnte, musste & the Frozen Pasts
lesson.subtitle: The preterite-present modals: konnte↔could, musste↔must — English froze their pasts into presents

hook.title: Pasts Wearing Present Clothes
hook.content: The six modal verbs are linguistic fossils with a scientific name: preterite-presents. Thousands of years ago their -te forms WERE past tenses — 'I could' meant 'I have been able'. Speakers re-read those pasts as presents, and the modals have lived in the present ever since. English did the exact same freeze and never thawed it: can and could are the same ancient word in two tenses, so are shall/should and will/would. And must? Must IS the old past tense of 'to matter' — grammatically a past that never left. German kept the whole system running: the modals' past tense is rebuilt with the ordinary dental -te — konnte, musste, durfte, sollte, wollte, wusste — one stem for every person, no vowel games at all.

footnotes.title: wist: the KJV Fossil
footnotes.content: English kept one frozen past as late as 1611: the King James Bible's 'they knew not nor wist' — wist is the old past of wit 'to know', the exact twin of German wusste. German wisst (you all know) and wissen still wear the same s that English buried.

pattern.title: One Weak Past, Six Ways
pattern.content: können → konnte ↔ could; müssen → musste ↔ must/had to; dürfen → durfte ↔ was allowed (archaic English durst!); sollen → sollte ↔ should; wollen → wollte ↔ wanted to; wissen → wusste ↔ knew (wist). Conjugation is boring on purpose: ich/er konnte, du konntest, wir konnten — one past stem for everybody, the dental -te doing all the work. And the bracket rule rides along: the bare infinitive stays at the end — Ich konnte nicht kommen, Ich musste gestern arbeiten, Wir wollten nach Berlin. Watch the trap: the double L of wollen survives into the past — wollte, du wolltest, wir wollten. Spell it with ll every time.
pattern.linguist_note: Preterite-presents go back to Proto-Indo-European perfect forms — old stative 'has-been-able' constructions re-anchored to the present. That is why the modals have no -en infinitive stress and no ge- participle in older speech: they were never ordinary verbs.

exercises.prompt: The frozen pasts — match each German modal past with its English twin:
exercises.target_answer: ich konnte, ich musste, ich wollte, ich wusste, ich durfte
exercises.meaning: I could, I had to, I wanted to, I knew, I was allowed
exercises.explanation: can/could, shall/should, will/would — English froze the same preterite-presents; musste is must's own frozen past, and durfte wears the weak dental -te like wollte.

exercises.prompt: Bracket check: 'Ich _____ nicht kommen.' (I couldn't come):
exercises.meaning: Ich konnte nicht kommen = I couldn't come
exercises.explanation: ich/er konnte — one past stem for every person, with the bare infinitive kommen at the bracket's end.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich _____ gestern arbeiten.' (I had to work yesterday):
exercises.meaning: Ich musste gestern arbeiten = I had to work yesterday
exercises.explanation: must has no living past of its own — but German musste is that past, still working.

exercises.prompt: wusste is the frozen past of which verb — the German 'to know'?
exercises.explanation: wissen freezes to wusste exactly as können freezes to konnte and müssen to musste — one weak -te past, one stem. schlagen and stehlen freeze differently — schlug, stahl — the ablaut melodies again.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the bracket: 'I couldn't come yesterday'
exercises.meaning: Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen = I couldn't come yesterday

vocab_hints.note: können's simple past — one stem, all persons

exercises.explanation: Modal past in position 2, bare infinitive at the end — the bracket survives the trip into the past intact.

summary.outcome: Use konnte, musste, durfte, sollte, wollte and wusste, and explain the preterite-present freeze behind English could/should/would.

use_example.german: Ich wollte kommen, aber ich musste arbeiten.
use_example.english: I wanted to come, but I had to work.

summary.takeaway: The modals are frozen pasts: konnte↔could, musste↔must, sollte↔should, wollte↔would, wusste↔wist — one weak -te past, one stem.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the dative case — methinks, mir and the giving case.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from konnte, musste & the Frozen Pasts (Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen = I couldn't come yesterday):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of konnte, musste & the Frozen Pasts without relying on short-term echo.

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

dürfen.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and p → f.

sollen.etymology_derivation: Direct twin of English "shall" and "should" (Shakespeare: "thou shalt" ↔ German "du sollst").

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

wünschen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunskijana — the page lists English wish as the direct cognate, both from the wish-love root *wen. [wiktionary]

schlagen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slahaną — English slay (Old English slēan) and slog are documented cognates; strong verb: schlug, geschlagen. [wiktionary]

stehlen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stelana, the same root as English steal; both keep the class-4 ablaut — steal, stole, stolen mirrors stehlen, stahl, gestohlen. [wiktionary]

jung.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *jungaz — the twin of English young (see der Junge). [wiktionary]

stark.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stark, Proto-West Germanic *stark; the everyday English word stark, as in stark naked, is the very same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schwach.context_phrase: Nach der Krankheit war er schwach.
schwach.context_translation: After the illness he was weak.
schwach.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swach, Proto-West Germanic *swak; the English cousins are the dialectal word swack, meaning nimble or lively, and Scots swack. [wiktionary]

gesund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sundaz — the same root as English sound, as in safe and sound. [wiktionary]

obwohl.context_phrase: Ich gehe laufen, obwohl es regnet.
obwohl.context_translation: I go running although it rains.
obwohl.etymology_derivation: Univerbation of ob (whether) and wohl (well — twin of English well); literally whether-well, hence although. English although is unrelated; the value here is the sentence-building role. [wiktionary]

japanisch.etymology_derivation: Japan + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Japanese. [wiktionary]
